endorsements.quote: We recommend AUPRC be reported for all prediction models [14].

Clinicians, not model developers, must decide the suitability of risk prediction models and their decision thresholds as they best understand the implications for clinical care, resource use and patient outcomes.

Concisely formulated alerts with suggested next actions, links to sepsis care pathways, and immediate feedback loops notifying model implementers of overrides or disagreements with model outputs all promote clinician acceptance [29].
Experience of groups who have successfully implemented risk prediction systems favours centralisation as being more efficient and acceptable to front-line clinicians [30, 31].

unlisted_practices: Do not rely on AUROC as the most salient measure of model accuracy for risk prediction models, especially when event prevalence is low.

Select model decision thresholds by jointly optimising effectiveness, efficiency (false alert burden) and utility (alert lead time before clinician suspicion), using a visual display of their interplay.
Assess alert timing relative to when clinicians already suspect the event and have initiated appropriate actions when evaluating prediction models.
Reduce false alert burden by raising thresholds in low-prevalence settings, excluding scenarios unrelated to the predicted risk, and temporarily switching the model off for certain patient groups.
Conduct bias analyses to determine whether a single base model should be retrained into sub-models for patient subsets with heterogeneous data density.

screen.reason: This is a commentary presenting framework methods and recommendations for clinicians to assess the fit-for-purpose status, decision thresholds, and alert configuration of AI-enabled risk prediction models in hospitals.
